title: Keshava Kashmiri
html:
The Conqueror of All Directions

In Sri Chaitanya's youth, when Nimai Pandita was the foremost teacher of Navadvipa, a famous scholar came to the town — a digvijayi, a “conqueror of all directions.” He had travelled all over India defeating pandits in debate and had come to defeat the celebrated scholars of Navadvipa as well; he left having given himself to the Lord's feet. The “Chaitanya-bhagavata” and the “Chaitanya-charitamrita” do not name him: in their verses he is only “the digvijayi,” “the great digvijayi,” “the poet,” “the brahmana.” The name comes from the commentaries. In the “Amrita-pravaha-bhashya” Srila Bhaktivinoda Thakura calls him Keshava Mishra of Kashmir; Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati in the “Anubhashya” calls him Keshava, a pandit from Kashmir, and in the “Gaudiya-bhashya” Keshava Bhatta, or Keshava Kashmiri. In the “Bhakti-ratnakara” he is Keshava Kashmir and also Laghu-Keshava, the “younger Keshava”; in Nabhadasa's “Bhaktamal” and in the Vallabhite “Varta” he is Keshava Bhatta with the byname “Kashmiri.” The biographies call him the digvijayi pandit Keshava Bhatta, “the invincible pandit,” and “the famous digvijayi Keshava Kashmiri.”1

That the digvijayi of the “Chaitanya-bhagavata” is Keshava Kashmiri Srila Bhaktisiddhanta gives in the “Gaudiya-bhashya” (on CB Adi 13.19) as the opinion of some, noting that on grounds of chronology opinions differ here; in the “Anubhashya” (on CC Adi 16.25) he calls the digvijayi Keshava without any reservation. It is this tradition of the Gaudiya Vaishnavas that we follow.2

Keshava came from Kashmir — “a most noble brahmana,” as the “Bhakti-ratnakara” says. The “Gaudiya-bhashya” names his teacher in the Nimbarka sampradaya as Gangala Bhatta, while the “Bhakti-ratnakara” calls Keshava the “beloved disciple” of Gokula Bhatta.3 The same “Bhakti-ratnakara” names Keshava Kashmiri the twenty-ninth in the line of disciples of Nimbaditya, that is, Sri Nimbarka; Srila Bhaktisiddhanta in the “Anubhashya” lists all twenty-nine names of this line — from Shrinivasacharya and Vishvacharya to Gopinatha, Keshava, Gokula and, last, Keshava Kashmiri. The sources give neither the year nor the place of his appearance, and his days are not found in the Vaishnava calendar of the Sri Chaitanya Saraswat Math.

Sarasvati's Blessing

Keshava was devoted heart and soul to Sarasvati and chanted her mantra without cease. She gave him her blessing: “You will conquer the three worlds!” All the sciences opened within him, his power grew, and going from land to land he defeated the scholars, so that he became renowned as a digvijayi. The “Bhakti-ratnakara” says the same: from the mantra of Sarasvati all knowledge came to him, and he became a conqueror of all directions.

But what is Sarasvati's blessing? Vrindavana Dasa Thakura says that Sarasvati is the very form of devotion to Vishnu; she is not different from Lakshmi and dwells on the Lord's chest. Her merciful glance can give a person devotion to Vishnu — so what difficulty is there for her in giving a scholar victory in debate? (CB Adi 13.21–23). The true Sarasvati is the highest knowledge, the Lord's internal energy; she hides herself from those blinded by pride and by the wish to be the doer and the enjoyer, and turns to them only through her shadow, which serves the Lord: such people receive worldly gifts from her and are deluded by them. But to one on whom her guileless glance falls she gives the highest good — devotion to Vishnu. The worldly fame of a world-conqueror is a trifle to her. So it was with Keshava: the blessing he took for his goal became only the road to the true fruit of his mantra.

With this gift Keshava wandered through the various lands of Bharatavarsha, wishing to defeat the pandits by his talent. Later he himself would list for the Lord where he had been: Gauda and Trihuta, Delhi and Kashi, Gujarat and Vijayanagara, Kanchi, Anga, Bengal, Andhra and Orissa — and everywhere the scholars could not even understand his words, let alone defeat him (CB Adi 13.160–162).

The Digvijayi in Navadvipa

Having defeated the assemblies of pandits in every kingdom, Keshava heard of the glory of Navadvipa, whose scholars were famed throughout India, and came in great pride to overcome them too. He did not come alone: he had servants, horses and elephants with him, and he carried a certificate of his victories over the scholars of every land of India (CB Adi 13.28, 13.30). When the pandits of Navadvipa learned that the great digvijayi had come, they were thrown into turmoil: alarm arose in every house and in every gathering of scholars. The “Bhakti-ratnakara” adds that the scholars of Chakhandi, too, lost their peace.

Krishnadasa Kaviraja places the meeting in time thus:

“Then came His marriage to Vishnupriya Thakurani, and after that the Lord's victory over the digvijayi, the conqueror of all directions.” (CC Adi 16.25)4

The students told Nimai about the digvijayi: he sat in a palanquin with a crowd of followers, elephants and horses, a victor's scroll in his hand; he was looking for a rival in Navadvipa, and if none were found he would demand that every assembly sign such a scroll for him (CB Adi 13.39–41).

Nimai answered them in words that Vrindavana Dasa preserved in the “Chaitanya-bhagavata”:

“When the Lord sees that someone is proud of his qualities, He takes away his cause for pride. A tree laden with fruit and a man adorned with good qualities bow down to the ground — the tree from the weight of its fruit, the man from humility. You have all heard of the great digvijayis of the past: Haihaya, Nahusha, Vena, Bana, Naraka and Ravana. Was there ever one who was not stripped of his pride? Know that the Supreme Lord lets no one remain proud. Very soon you will all see how here, in Navadvipa, the digvijayi's pride will be broken.” (CB Adi 13.44–48)5

That evening, seated on the Ganga's bank among His students, the Lord thought to Himself not of how to defeat the guest but of how to save him. If He overcame him before everyone, He reasoned, the disgrace would be like death to him: people would mock him, plunder his goods, and he himself would die of grief. So the Lord resolved to defeat him away from the crowd — to crush his pride and spare him unbearable pain (CB Adi 13.53–57). The full moon rose. Keshava came to the bank, bowed to the Ganga, and asked one of the students who this youth was, shining with extraordinary beauty: “This is the famous Nimai Pandita.” And the conqueror of so many assemblies, seeing the Lord, felt timid (CB Adi 13.58–75; CC Adi 16.28–29).

The Verses on the Ganga

The Lord received the guest with respect and gave him a seat of honour. But he, as the “Charitamrita” tells, answered Him with disdain:

“You teach grammar, and Your name is Nimai Pandita. People praise Your skill in the science that children learn. Of the grammars, I know, You teach the Kalapa, and I have heard of Your students' debates on its tricky points.” (CC Adi 16.31–32)

The Lord humbly called Himself a child who had only just begun to study, and him an expert in every shastra and a poet, and asked him to glorify the sacred Ganga in verse. The “Chaitanya-bhagavata” gives His request thus:

“O pandit, great is your poetic gift! There is no subject you could not sing. Please tell us in verse of the glory of the Ganga; hearing of it, anyone may be cleansed of sin.” (CB Adi 13.77–78)

Keshava at once began to compose verses and recited them without pause, swift as the wind; his voice thundered like thunder in the clouds, and all were struck dumb, amazed at his gift. According to the “Charitamrita,” within a single ghati — some twenty-four minutes — he composed a hundred shlokas in praise of the Ganga.6 The Lord praised him: in all the world there is no poet like him — and, to Keshava's astonishment, recited one of the hundred shlokas by heart:

“This greatness of the Ganga ever shines beyond compare, for she is blessed by her birth from the lotus feet of Sri Vishnu. Like a second Sri Lakshmi, she receives the worship of gods and men; and upon the head of Bhavani's husband she reigns, endowed with wondrous qualities.” (CC Adi 16.41)

Amazed, Keshava asked how He had managed to retain even one verse when he had recited them as fast as the wind. The Lord replied: by the grace of a deity you have become a great poet, and by the grace of a deity another remembers everything at a single hearing (CC Adi 16.42–44).

He asked him to explain the verse and then asked about its merits and faults. Vrindavana Dasa writes that no sooner had the digvijayi begun to explain than the Lord pointed out flaws at the beginning, in the middle and at the end:

“The Lord said, ‘These ornaments of sound (shabda-alankaras) are contrived and strange; their use departs from what the shastras accept. Tell us, what meaning did you put into these ornaments?’” (CB Adi 13.94–95)

The detailed analysis that Vrindavana Dasa does not give is supplied by Krishnadasa Kaviraja: in this one shloka the Lord found five faults and five poetic ornaments (CC Adi 16.45–86).7

The son of Sarasvati was bewildered. He answered at random, and Gaurasundara found a flaw in every argument he made:

“It seemed that his reason had left the digvijayi, for he himself did not understand what he was saying.” (CB Adi 13.98)

The Lord proposed to leave that verse aside and hear another, but Keshava could no longer speak as before (CB Adi 13.99).

Keshava thought that Sarasvati herself was speaking through the youth's mouth, and asked how He, never having studied poetics, could give such an explanation. The “Charitamrita” continues:

“Hearing this, Mahaprabhu, who dearly loved a jest, read his heart and answered playfully: ‘Whether My analysis of the shastras is good or bad, I Myself do not know. I only speak the words that Sarasvati makes Me speak.’ Hearing this, the digvijayi concluded, ‘The goddess has defeated me through a child.’” (CC Adi 16.93–95)

The Lord's words are a jest: He does not depend on Sarasvati — He is her Lord and Husband, as she herself would tell Keshava that same night. Keshava, for his part, resolved to pray to the goddess that very day and ask her why she had humbled him through a child. And Krishnadasa Kaviraja reveals what had really happened:

“In truth, it was Sarasvati who had him compose a faulty verse, and when it was examined she clouded his intelligence.” (CC Adi 16.97)

The students could barely hold back their laughter, but the Lord did not let them laugh. He encouraged the guest in every way: He called him the crest-jewel of poets, said that faults can be found even in Bhavabhuti, Jayadeva and Kalidasa, asked him not to take His boyish impudence to heart, and bade him rest, consult his books in the night and return on the morrow (CC Adi 16.98–104; CB Adi 13.108–117). So the Lord dealt with everyone He defeated: He offended no one, and the scholars of Navadvipa loved Him.

This was no worldly contest of learning. Krishnadasa Kaviraja opens the chapter by saying that Sarasvati honoured the youthful Chaitanya, taking His victory over the digvijayi as her occasion (CC Adi 16.3). Sarasvati herself made the shloka imperfect, and the Lord, having prevailed, did not humiliate the defeated man. His victory was mercy.

But Keshava did not yet know this. Deeply ashamed and in great sorrow he thought: “I have defeated matchless masters of the six darshanas — Nyaya, Sankhya, Yoga, Mimamsa, Vaisheshika and Vedanta — and today by ill fate I am beaten by a youthful teacher of nothing more than grammar, a science for children! Perhaps I have lost Sarasvati's blessing, or offended her feet.”

Sarasvati's Revelation

Chanting Sarasvati's mantra, the sorrowful Keshava fell asleep, and that very night she appeared to him in a dream.8 She revealed to him a great secret: Nimai Pandita is not some common mortal pandit but the all-powerful Bhagavan Himself. And she who had given Keshava his victories is only a shadow (chhaya-shakti) of the highest knowledge, the Lord's own internal energy (svarupa-shakti); this shadow Sarasvati feels shame to come before Narayana and abides solely as dependent on Him. Vrindavana Dasa gives her words:

“Know that the youth who defeated you is none other than the Lord of countless universes Himself. I am the eternal maidservant of His lotus feet, and I am ashamed to appear before Him.” (CB Adi 13.129–130)

She called this a secret of the Vedas and warned him that to divulge it would shorten his life. The youth, she said, is the Lord of countless universes; He was Matsya and Kurma, Varaha, Nrisimha and Vamana, Rama; He is known as the son of Vasudeva and of Nanda, and now He has come as the son of a brahmana (CB Adi 13.127–143).

And she said further that now at last he had gained the real fruit of his mantra:

“The title of digvijayi is not the true fruit of your chanting and of your worship of me. The true fruit of your chanting and worship is that you have been able to see the Lord, the Master of countless universes. Therefore, O brahmana, go at once and take shelter at His lotus feet.” (CB Adi 13.145–147)

Do not take this for a mere dream, she said, and do not disregard my words: won over by the power of your mantra, I have revealed to you what the Vedas keep hidden (CB Adi 13.148).

With these words she vanished. So Sarasvati herself turned her worshipper away from herself to the Lord: the fruit of worshipping her is not the gifts of this world but shelter at the feet of the One whom she serves.

At the Lord's Feet

On waking, Keshava went straight to the Lord. He bowed down, and the Lord raised him and embraced him. The Lord asked what such behaviour meant, and Keshava answered that the cause was His merciful glance. “But you are a digvijayi yourself,” said the Lord, “why do you speak to Me like this?” (CB Adi 13.152–153). With many humble entreaties Keshava told Him his dream and Sarasvati's instruction, and said:

“You are the Supreme Person, Lord Narayana; yet You have appeared in the age of Kali as a brahmana. Who can know You? … You defeated me three times, and yet You did not humiliate me. Is this possible for anyone but the Supreme Lord? You are surely Lord Narayana Himself.” (CB Adi 13.155, 158–159)

You are the Husband and Lord of Sarasvati, he said, she herself told me so. At a most auspicious hour he had come to Navadvipa and seen the Lord — he who was drowning in the well of worldly life, bewitched by ignorance and desire, deceiving himself. And he prayed: “Free me by Your merciful glance … instruct me, so that no material desire remains in my heart” (CB Adi 13.164–169).

The Lord, the Master of Sarasvati, instructed him:

“Knowledge should not be used to conquer the world; knowledge has value only in the service of the Supreme Lord. … Therefore, O brahmana, give up your worldly ambitions and devote yourself wholly to the service of Sri Krishna's lotus feet. … Know, then, that the fruit of true knowledge is unshakable faith that the real wealth of the heart lies hidden at Krishna's lotus feet.” (CB Adi 13.173, 176, 178)

The higher knowledge, which leads to the Lord's service, is precious; the lower knowledge, pursued for victories and worldly fame, is worthless.

With these words the Lord embraced the brahmana warmly, and he was freed from all bonds. “Give up your pride, worship Krishna, be merciful to all living beings,” the Lord told him (CB Adi 13.180–182). The “Charitamrita” says the same briefly:

“In the morning he came and took shelter at the Lord's feet, and the Lord showed him mercy and cut his bonds.” (CC Adi 16.107)

And Vrindavana Dasa himself, listing the pastimes of the Adi-khanda, says that Gauranga defeated the digvijayi and then freed him from all bonds (CB Adi 1.114). The Lord strictly forbade him to reveal to anyone what Sarasvati had told him: secrets more hidden than the Vedas are not to be divulged (CB Adi 13.183–184). Prostrating himself again and again at His feet, Keshava went away feeling that he had attained the greatest good fortune (CB Adi 13.185–186).

Through the Lord's mercy there awoke in Keshava's heart, all at once, devotion, detachment and knowledge. Having attained the highest devotion, he felt that his life had reached its goal, and not a trace was left of the digvijayi's pride: he became “humbler than a blade of grass” (CB Adi 13.187–188). This humility is not worldly modesty but the fruit of mercy, as is his detachment: his elephants, horses, palanquins and riches he gave away to worthy people and, wholly detached, continued his wanderings (CB Adi 13.189–190). The “Bhakti-ratnakara” says that, leaving everything, he went away at the Lord's command. “Thus the digvijayi obtained release,” Vrindavana Dasa concludes (CB Adi 13.197). The one the Lord defeated was not humiliated — he was set free.

Krishnadasa Kaviraja sums it up:

“The digvijayi was fortunate, and his life bore fruit: through his learning he attained the feet of Mahaprabhu.” (CC Adi 16.108)

And the pandits of Navadvipa, seeing Nimai's extraordinary power, wished to confer on Him jointly the title “Vadi-simha” (“a lion among debaters”); and His fame spread far and wide (CB Adi 13.198–205; “Bhakti-ratnakara” 2.250–252).

How Others Tell It

Krishnadasa Kaviraja acknowledges that Vrindavana Dasa Thakura was the first to describe this story at length, but did not set out clearly the merits and faults of the digvijayi's verse; therefore, bowing to him, the author of the “Charitamrita” gives that analysis (CC Adi 16.26–27).

In Narahari Chakravarti's “Bhakti-ratnakara” the victory over the digvijayi is recalled by Chaitanya Dasa, telling his son Shrinivasa of the Lord's pastimes he had witnessed in his youth. The proud logicians of Navadvipa laughed at the Lord, and Chaitanya Dasa prayed to the Creator to crush their pride; and then:

“Suddenly a digvijayi came to Navadvipa; before his might everyone trembled. The goddess Sarasvati is subject to his devotion; therefore he is a great poet and expert in the shastras.” (“Bhakti-ratnakara” 2.237–238)

“At that time Narayana, the Husband of Sarasvati, named Nimai Pandita, was teaching grammar.” (2.241)

The digvijayi approached Him, laughing in the pride of his learning, and in a moment composed many shlokas; the Lord pointed out errors in one of them,9 honoured the defeated man, Sarasvati revealed to him who the Lord was, and he surrendered at His feet. After that, says Chaitanya Dasa, his teacher and all the other scholars ceased to regard Nimai as a mere man (“Bhakti-ratnakara” 2.243–252).

Govinda Deva in the “Gaura-krishnodaya” tells how on a moonlit night a learned digvijayi, a thunder-voiced poet full of envy, came to the Lord; he praised the Ganga in a hundred verses, and the Lord, retaining one at a single hearing, found in it many hidden faults and five evident ones. Returning to his lodging, the digvijayi fasted and at midnight propitiated the goddess, and she, laughing, said:

“Why do you grieve at being humbled by the Lord of all? Hundreds of learned Sarasvatis serve Him; I am His maidservant; what then of you!” (“Gaura-krishnodaya” 5.25)

At the end of the night the aged brahmana came to the Lord and took shelter of His feet, and the Lord, instructing him in the truth about Himself, saved him (“Gaura-krishnodaya” 5.11–27). This is the only source that speaks of Keshava's age: by then he was already old.

Other poets, too, mention this victory briefly. Jayananda writes in his “Chaitanya-mangala”: “Then the Lord defeated the conqueror of the quarters and at last destroyed all his bonds.” In a pada of Narahari, Gaura is glorified as the One who “conquered the digvijayi,” to whom the pandits of Nadia submit (“Gaura-charita-chintamani” 10.17). The biographies recall Keshava in the stories of other companions as well: before His initiation at Gaya, Mahaprabhu was a pandit of grammar, prosody and logic and defeated the invincible Keshava Kashmiri; He could hold of no account the learning of all the famous pandits — not only His neighbours, but the renowned digvijayi Keshava Kashmiri himself.

Keshava is remembered beyond Bengal too. Nabhadasa in the “Bhaktamal” (c. 1600) praises Keshava Bhatta with the byname “Kashmiri”: with the firm axe of devotion to Hari he felled the trees of other dharmas, and in Mathura he overcame the mlecchas in debate, so that the qazis, never before defeated, were filled with fear (chhappay 75). Of the meeting with Mahaprabhu Nabhadasa is silent. Priyadasa, however, tells it in his kavittas on the “Bhaktamal”: Keshava comes to Nadia with palanquin, elephants and horses; Mahaprabhu Himself approaches him on the bank of the Ganga; Keshava composes a hundred shlokas; the Lord repeats one and, asked how He remembered it, answers, “He who gave you the power gave [it] to Me too,” and then analyses its faults and merits. Back at his lodging, Keshava meditates on Sarasvati and, when she comes, reproaches her: “You let me conquer the whole world — and let me be defeated by a boy!” Sarasvati answers, “He is my Lord, Bhagavan”; the Lord tells him, “Sir, take the fruit — bhakti; defeat no one any more …,” and Keshava leaves his retinue and pomp behind. The next kavitta tells of his victory over the Muslims at Vishram Ghat in Mathura.10

The tradition of Vallabha's followers mentions Keshava as well.11

In the Line of Nimbarka

Having been defeated by Sri Gaurasundara, Keshava understood who Sriman Mahaprabhu is and, in order to serve the Lord, entered the Nimbarka sampradaya — so writes Srila Bhaktisiddhanta in the “Anubhashya.” Srila Bhaktivinoda Thakura in the “Amrita-pravaha-bhashya” says that, having received instruction from Mahaprabhu, he became an acharya in the sampradaya of Nimbaditya.

In the “Gaudiya-bhashya” Srila Bhaktisiddhanta explains this further. Accepting Gaurasundara's instruction, Keshava gave up his former conclusions drawn from the six darshanas and by the Lord's mercy remembered Nimbarka's ten verses, the “Dasha-shloki.” The instruction to serve Radha-Govinda awakened in him the sentiments of his predecessors in that line, to whom he had earlier, seeking the fame of a digvijayi, been indifferent (on CB Adi 13.175–177). The Lord, Bhaktisiddhanta writes, crushed the pride of the Kashmiri digvijayi Keshavacharya, cleansed his heart of the worship of worldly learning and instructed him in the highest truth — inconceivable oneness and difference (achintya-bheda-abheda), whose essence is the service of Radha-Govinda; Gaurasundara honoured him with the rank of a Vaishnava acharya (on CB Adi 1.114). Keshava himself could compose verses instantly in any metre.

To him belongs the “Kaustubha-prabha,” a commentary on Shrinivasacharya's “Vedanta-kaustubha,” the exposition of Nimbarka's bhashya on the “Vedanta-sutra,” the “Vedanta-parijata-saurabha.” According to Srila Bhaktivinoda, he wrote commentaries on the “Vedanta-parijata” and other bhashyas.

The “Krama-dipika” is a harder question. Srila Gopala Bhatta Gosvami in the “Hari-bhakti-vilasa” and the commentary “Dig-darshini” cite many proofs from the works of Keshava Bhatta, the author of the “Krama-dipika.” In the “Gaudiya-bhashya” on CB Adi 13.19 Srila Bhaktisiddhanta remarks that this Keshava Bhatta was later entered as an acharya in the guru-parampara of the Nimbarka sampradaya; but had the author of the “Krama-dipika” belonged to Nimbarka's line, the author of the “Hari-bhakti-vilasa” might well have said so. In other places of the “Gaudiya-bhashya” he names Keshava outright as the compiler of the “Krama-dipika”: Sanatana and Gopala Bhatta saw in him a recipient of Mahaprabhu's mercy and therefore took material from the “Krama-dipika” for the smriti of the Gaudiya Vaishnavas.12

The “Bhakti-ratnakara,” in its twelfth wave, listing the line of Nimbaditya, says that the digvijayi Keshava Kashmir, ashamed, … [was known] by the name “Laghu-Keshava,” and that the fortunate Keshava Kashmir was immersed in inexpressible joy.13 His name also appears in the list in the “Vaishnava-manjusha” (issue 1).

Of what came after, Srila Bhaktisiddhanta writes in the “Gaudiya-bhashya” as follows. Later Keshava and other scholars from Kashmir, his followers, left the shelter of Mahaprabhu and went their own way, founding an independent sampradaya (on CB Adi 13.175–177). And Keshava's present-day so-called followers claim that he was Mahaprabhu's vartma-pradarshaka-guru — the one who first showed Him the path. That, says Bhaktisiddhanta, is why — to save such people from offence — Vrindavana Dasa writes that the Lord “destroyed all his bonds” (on CB Adi 1.114): it was not Keshava who gave knowledge to the Lord, but the Lord — the Teacher of all the worlds — who set Keshava free.

His Departure

Of Keshava's later life the primary sources are silent. The time and place of his departure from this world are not known: no source names them, and his days are not found in the Vaishnava calendar of the Sri Chaitanya Saraswat Math.

Significance

The story of Keshava Kashmiri is a lesson about knowledge. The Lord always takes away pride, while true worth is humble, like a tree bowed down by the weight of its fruit. Knowledge that serves victories and worldly fame is worthless; the fruit of learning is a heart and wealth offered at Krishna's feet. Keshava sought the fame of a world-conqueror and found what is higher than all victories: “through his learning he attained the feet of Mahaprabhu.”

And it is a lesson about mercy. Sarasvati, whom he worshipped, herself sent him on to her Lord; the Lord defeated him so as not to humiliate him, and with a single embrace gave him devotion, detachment and knowledge all at once. The one the Lord defeats is not humiliated but set free.

Notes

  1. In the Bengali text of the verses of the “Charitamrita” he has no name — only “the digvijayi,” “the poet,” “the brahmana”; in the Russian translation of these verses the name Keshava Kashmiri has been brought into the text from the commentaries. He should not be confused with his namesakes: Keshava Bharati, who gave the Lord sannyasa; the sannyasi Keshava Puri; Keshava Vasu (Keshava Chhatri), an official of the sultan of Gauda; and Keshava Samanta of Medinipur.
  2. The Nimbarka tradition places Keshava Kashmiri in another period and does not accept his meeting with Mahaprabhu. We follow the “Charitamrita,” the “Chaitanya-bhagavata” and Srila Bhaktisiddhanta. On the “Krama-dipika,” see below, note 12.
  3. According to the “Bhakti-ratnakara,” Gokula Bhatta was a disciple of Keshava Bhatta, and he of Gopinatha Bhatta. In the “Gaudiya-bhashya” (on CB Adi 13.175) Gangalya Bhatta is named first among the disciples of the compiler of the “Krama-dipika.” We do not attempt to reconcile these accounts.
  4. The “Chaitanya-bhagavata” tells of the digvijayi in Adi 13 — before the Lord's journey to East Bengal and before His second marriage (Adi 14–15); the “Charitamrita” places the victory after the marriage to Vishnupriya. The biographies say only that it happened when Nimai was the foremost teacher of Navadvipa.
  5. In one of the biographies a misprint puts another word in place of Ravana in this list.
  6. According to the “Chaitanya-bhagavata,” he recited without stopping for a whole prahara — about three hours; one of the biographies says the same. The “Gaura-krishnodaya” and Priyadasa, like the “Charitamrita,” speak of a hundred verses.
  7. The “Chaitanya-bhagavata” speaks of flaws “at the beginning, in the middle and at the end” (Adi 13.93), one of the biographies of countless flaws; the “Gaura-krishnodaya” (5.21) of many hidden and five evident faults, the chief of them avimrishta-vidheyamsha, a faulty word order that obscures the main statement. We follow the “Charitamrita.”
  8. According to the “Charitamrita” (Adi 16.105–106), that night he worshipped Sarasvati and she instructed him; according to the “Gaura-krishnodaya” (5.24–25), he fasted and at midnight propitiated the goddess; according to Priyadasa, Sarasvati appeared to him while he was awake, meditating on her. We follow the “Chaitanya-bhagavata.”
  9. The “Bhakti-ratnakara” speaks of three errors; the “Charitamrita” of five faults (Adi 16.45–86).

According to the “Vallabha-varta” (baithak 13, Govinda-kunda), “Krishna-Chaitanya” and Keshava Bhatta Kashmiri stood beside Vallabha, and neither could read the handwriting of the Svamini, Sri Radha, in the book “Krishna-premamrita”; Vallabha gave the book to Krishna-Chaitanya and not to Keshava. This is a tradition of the Pushti-marga, formed in another school. For the Gaudiya Vaishnavas Mahaprabhu is Krishna Himself in the mood and with the complexion of Radha, and we do not include this story in his life.
